newsitem.title: UK: Most UK finance directors oppose ACT cut - poll.
newsitem.headline: Most UK finance directors oppose ACT cut - poll.

text.p: Nearly three-quarters of British finance directors are opposed to measures to reduce or scrap share dividend tax credits widely expected in the July 2 budget, according to a poll published on Thursday.
Recruitment agency Reed Accountancy Personnel asked over 200 finance directors for their views on changes to advance corporation tax (ACT).

Seventy-one percent said they would object to any reduction, arguing that it would raise the cost of final salary pension schemes and cause some companies to switch to money purchase schemes. Some felt it would have a serious impact on the UK investment industry and damage pension funds.

"Financial directors believe strongly that the tax-exempt institutes such as pension funds, charities and some insurance funds will bear the brunt of the changes in dividend tax credit rules," said Reed Accountancy Personnel deputy chairman Derek Beal.

"The prospect of millions of UK workers facing double taxation, plus the difficulties which companies may face in keeping employee pension funds in credit as a result, have simply served to turn by far the majority of the UK's financial bosses against the proposal."
A reduction in ACT is widely expected to top Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's list of revenue-raising measures in his first budget.

Companies pay ACT on their dividend payments to cover shareholders' tax liabilities but can deduct the money from their corporation tax bill. Tax-exempt shareholders can then claim a refund on the dividend tax paid on their behalf.
ACT abolition could save the Treasury about five billion sterling while a reduction to 10 percent from the current 20 percent should garner roughly three billion pounds.
Twelve percent of finance directors polled agreed with plans to scrap ACT, while 17 percent were neutral on the issue.
